blocks.text: My bare foot slaps down on cold stone, and the gallery laughs.

It rolls down off the rail above us, a hundred people at once, the laugh you'd give a dog in a hat. I'm the only Damper in the Cellar Ring who plays barefoot. A hundred people in Kilnyard have just found out.
Behind me, Dov is studying the ceiling as if he has never met me.
One person in the front row isn't laughing. She's wearing more money than the whole Kilnyard side earns in a year, and she's staring at my toes.
"Three things," says Sef, at my right shoulder, where I can hear him. "One, that's Callista Veyne. Last Plate for House Veyne. Choir side."
"What's a Choir Damper doing in a lime kiln?"

"Two. The Warden walked her to that seat himself and bowed. So she's here for the Chapter. Scouting." His pencil runs across the page without his eyes following it. "Three. Scouts write everything down. She hasn't written a word."

She hasn't. Grey gloves folded in her lap. No book, no pencil. Pale hair pinned flat as a plumb line. She watches my feet cross from the first stand to the second the way I used to watch a lintel lowered onto its bed. I don't watch those any more.
"Ignore her," says Dov. "Everyone else is ignoring you. I'm ignoring you."
"You're talking to me."
"I'm talking near you. It's different."

Home floor. I know every stand in this Drum by knuckle, which one rings bright, which one's a hair proud of its neighbour, which one has a vein of something darker running through it like a crack that never opened. Bare, they're colder than Ropewalk's and closer-grained. The bloom is beaten up thick enough to taste, and the gallery's feet come down through the walls into my heels.
Marten takes the stand beside mine. His hands are open again. He Grounded his four out the night after Ropewalk, humming, and he hasn't said one word about my late draw. That's worse than if he had.
The Warden swings his tell-weight. "Pace five."
Sef registers Marten and me as Dampers. Oduya, at the plate rail, rests her fingers on our Last Plate's peg the way a cook rests a hand on a pot lid.
Across the floor, Dyeworks come out in stained aprons. Their first Caller is a tall woman with hands dyed blue to the wrist.

"Perpetua Fenwick," says Sef. "Indigo. She bends. The big lad beside her I'm calling Mangle. Throws straight and heavy and not often. Four things. One, stay on your stands. Two, I don't know yet. Three, I'll tell you when I do. Four, don't look at the Veyne woman."
I look at the Veyne woman. She's still looking at my feet.
Indigo's first Raise.

Her lead-in comes up through my soles, clean, a hand-width under our peg. I've got this floor's chart in my knuckles. For that pitch, at pace five, there's a pair: Marten's stand and the one on the ash-door side of it, a pace and four-tenths apart along her line.
"Marten. Ash-door side."
I step across. He sets his feet. The Raise ends. She voices.
The glow comes crawling at walking pace, slow as a man crossing a room. And halfway across the Drum the floor slides under my feet.
That's the only way I can say it. The pitch in my soles climbs, like a cart wheel finding a slope. She's bending it. In flight. Paying double weight for every hair of the climb.
Two semitones moves the half-wave by about a seventh of a pace. The null forgives a tenth.
"Off!"
Neither of us draws. The note shoves through Marten, then me, a three that arrives a one, and strikes our Last Plate dead on the peg. Three counts of our own plate singing at us.
Nought to one.
"She's chasing my peg," says Oduya, very low, which is worse than shouting. "In the air. The cheek of it."
On their fourth throw Indigo does it again. Lead-in under the peg. I pick the pair for it. The floor slides. "Off!" Through us both. A one, still on the peg. Still a Peal.
Nought to two. The gallery likes this a great deal.
Dov answers with the Lamplighter, high and hard, and tells the gallery its name as it rings. One to two. He bows. Nobody claps. He bows anyway.
"Interesting," says Sef, and then nothing, for a whole Breath.

Then: "Three things. One. A bent three costs her six. She's spent twelve on two Peals. Two. A Caller's got about thirty in a match. Three. She knows that, and she's still doing it, because it's working."
It's working because every pair I pick from her lead-in is wrong by the time the note gets here. I'm picking for where she starts. I need where she finishes.
I stand on the cold stone and go back over it with my eyes shut.

In warm-up she hummed her scales across the floor, and every scale ended with a little lift at the top. I felt it and thought nothing of it. Then the first Peal: two semitones up. Then the second: two semitones up. Not one and a half. Not a lazy one. Two, both times, exact to the quarter-tone.
Stone that cracks the same way three times isn't unlucky. It has a fault in its bed. Hers is a habit. She learned to bend at one size and she never learned another.
So I don't pick for the lead-in. I pick for the lead-in plus two.
If I'm wrong, if she throws this one straight, Marten and I double a three. A Mark each, in the Book forever, and Marten has four left.
"Marten." I turn so he's square in front of me, and I make my mouth big. "Next one of hers, I count it. You draw on my count. Not the light. My count."
He looks at my mouth a long moment. Then at my eyes.
"Aye, well," he says.

Mangle throws in between, straight and heavy. Oduya has walked our peg a semitone in the Breath before his Raise, so his note goes through us both and rattles like a dropped tray. Indigo waits a throw. Then her hand goes up.

Lead-in, up through the soles. A hand-width under the peg again. Add two. At pace five that's a wave of about two and a half paces. Half of that is a pace and a quarter. There's one pair on this floor that spacing along her line: the ash-door stand and the one just inside it.
"Inside!"
Marten steps. I step. The Raise ends.
She voices. The glow crawls. Halfway, the floor slides up under me, two semitones, and lands inside our band like a block dropping onto its bed. True.
"Three," I say, to his face. "Two. Draw."
I don't hold back. It isn't that I trust him. It's my count; there's nothing to check. He's the one doing the trusting. I know which side of that bargain is easier.
We draw.
Palms out, a breath in. The glow goes out between us like a pinched wick.
Nothing comes into my hands. No ring. Not a hum in my ears, not a tingle in my fingers. There's just a hole in the air where a note was, and behind us our Last Plate hanging silent on its chain.
Dead air.

The gallery doesn't know what it saw. For a count there's nothing. Then somebody shouts, "Ghost!" and the rest take it up, laughing, stamping on the rail. Ghost quell. Luck. The barefoot one got lucky.
The Warden crosses with his rod. He sets its foot on my stand, holds it, lifts it. Sets it on Marten's.
"Nothing, Halloway," he says. "Nothing, Sallow."
He frowns at the rod as if it owes him money and walks back to his weight.
In the front row Callista Veyne has not moved at all. Her lips have come apart.
Marten is looking at his own palms.
I'm standing on my stand with no ring in me at all, toes flat on the stone, when something comes up through it.
Knock. Knock. Knock.
Then nothing. A pause about as long as a breath, held open.

Not settling stone. I know how stone settles. It goes once, or it goes in a grumble, and it never goes in time. This is three, evenly spaced, like a knuckle on a door. Like mine on a flag, asking if it's sound.
The last time I felt anything under this floor I had five ring in my bones and hands I couldn't close. Tonight I've got nothing in me. Nothing, Halloway.
"Wren!"
Sef. In my good ear. He's been saying it for a while.
"Gap side! Wren!"

Mangle's hand is up. The Raise is ending. My heel lifts to move, and I stop it in the air. The Raise is over; moving now is hush-stepping, and hush-stepping is a penalty Peal. I set the heel back down on my stand like a cup on a saucer.
Mangle's note goes through Marten alone, four to three, and strikes our plate a semitone and a half off Oduya's peg. Rattle. Nothing.
It should have been through two of us.
Sef is looking at me. Not the "interesting" look. A worse one, with no word in it.
"Cold feet," I say. "What's next?"
He holds the look one count longer. "Indigo's next."
I put the knock where I've been putting things. With the voice. With the bond. With the lintel. Later.
Indigo's hand goes up. Lead-in plus two. The ash-door pair again.
"Three. Two. Draw."
The glow pinches out between Marten and me. The gallery shouts "Ghost!" again, less sure of itself. The Warden reads nothing off either stand.
This time I don't wait to feel the floor. I keep my eyes on Sef.
Dov's Mordant rings on the last throw before the Half, a low, dirty, staining sort of note, he says, named for the occasion. Two all.
At the Long Ground we hum ourselves down to nothing, which for Marten and me tonight is no distance at all.
"Wren Halloway," says Oduya, passing behind me, "your toes are the colour of a plum skin. Keep them moving or I will boil them."
Dov drops onto his heels in front of my stand and looks at my feet as if they've been rude to him. "You're still doing the feet thing."
"I'm still doing the feet thing."
"Fine," he says, as if it costs him a crown. "Do it more."

"Three things," Sef says, crouched by my stand. "One. Indigo has spent twenty-four. She bends once more and she's cracked for a week. Two. So it's Mangle all Half. Three." He looks at my feet. "Can you do it on straight ones?"
Straight ones are easy. A straight note is exactly what its lead-in says it is. All it needs is a pair on the floor chart, a wave of five paces or less, and two people drawing in the same instant.
"Watch," I say.
Mangle throws heavy, and his notes run high enough. A three-pace wave. A pair a pace and a half apart, on the Last Plate side. I count it into Marten's face. Dead air.
The gallery doesn't shout this time.

Dov, meanwhile, is having the night of his life. He throws the Long Goodnight, which floats and then drops onto their peg like a cat off a wall. Three to two. He throws the Widowmaker, the high one that bends at the very end. Their Damper steps into it to block, and it goes through her and rings anyway. Four to two.
Mangle's last hard note comes at us with eight throws left in the Half. A four-pace wave, the edge of what this floor can do. Two paces apart, Marten's stand and mine, across the dark vein.
"Three. Two. Draw."
Out like a wick.
Four ghost quells. Up on the rail somebody says, quite loud, "That's not luck," and nobody laughs at him.
Dov Peals his fifth on the last throw of the night and names it after himself.
Five to two.

The Warden calls the result. Both Scribes put their hands to his sheet. Sef presses a crown into my hand on the stair without looking at it. Four of thirty-eight, once it's in the tin. A third of the Run gone. Thirty-four to find.
Dov flings an arm round my neck in front of the whole gallery. "Wren's with me," he tells them. "I taught Wren everything."
"You told me to put my boots on."
"Everything except that."
I take my boots up the stair in my hand. The kiln door at the top lets out onto frost, and the frost feels like knives after the stone, which is fine. I want something simple in my feet for a minute.
Someone steps out of the dark on my left.
"Other side," I say.
"I beg your pardon?"
"Other side. If you want me to hear you."
Callista Veyne considers this as if it were a rule she hadn't read yet. Then she walks round to my right, keeping exactly the distance she'd keep from a puddle.
Up close she's younger than her coat. Her gloves are twisted together in front of her, very tight.
"You stand like a mason tiling a scullery," she says. "Barefoot, in a cellar, in winter. It's almost charming."
"I am a mason."
"Yes. That's the charming part."
"Did the Chapter send you to look at my toes," I say, "or is that your own hobby? Because the gallery charges a penny either way."
She doesn't smile. "Four ghost quells. One night. One floor. I have read the Warden's sheets for every Cellar Ring Run for three years. Nobody has had two in a night."
"Lucky floor."
"Were you holding ring?"
"None. Ask the Warden. He said 'nothing' twice."

"None," she says, as if the word were a rule she'd misread. Her gloves twist tighter. Her eyes go past me, down the stair, toward the Drum, and stay there a moment too long. She looks, very briefly, like somebody standing on a stair waiting for a note to reach her.
"After the first one," she says, "you stopped. You stood on that stand as if someone had said your name."
"Cold feet."
She takes one step closer. She's exact about it, as if the distance were in the rulebook.
"You felt that," says Callista Veyne. "Don't lie. I watched your feet."
